doc.title: Tim Ries interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, March 19, 2022

title: Recording with Elvin Jones and declining his road offer
summary: Ries recounts a session with Elvin Jones, Gary Bartz, Christian McBride and Roseanna Vitro, and regrets not giving his number when invited on the road.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: My first record date: sessions, personnel, discography

blocks.x: Wow. 60 years. You’ve played with a lot of other pop artists we’ll call it. If you have Spotify on or Sirius radio things come on the radio and you go, “I think I was on that.” Does that happen to you?

It has, where I’ll be like, “Oh yeah I forgot about doing that.” It has happened where like I think that — is that even me? You know like it could be me. Because I did a lot of recordings in New York with different acts and different performers and artists and stuff. And I often remember most things but then yeah, something slips. Yeah I did that or even — but it’s kind of a cool thing to have the experience of performing with so many people over the years and, you know, being influenced by their music and then getting a chance like to play — like I got a chance to record with Elvin Jones who is like arguably one of the greatest musicians who ever lived on any instrument, but then — and I haven’t told this ever publicly but a couple of my close friends know this but again, like until I was 50 accepting people saying we enjoyed the night and I can say thank you. When I recorded with Elvin he said, “Well I’m going on the road soon, make sure you give my wife your information because we would like to take you on the road. Now this was in my 30s. What I heard was you record with John Coltrane. What could I possibly do? I did not go, I did not give her my number, because I was like I’m not ready. So I got a chance to play with him but I didn’t travel with him and I look back at that as like one of the greatest mistakes of my life because it was like he must have heard something that was, you know, enough for him to say would you like to go on the road with us. And I was like man, but at that time in my life I was like well I’m not ready for this gig. It’s Elvin Jones. But now I look at it and you know he’s not here anymore and it’s like — you know so I wouldn’t make that same choice.
Would that have been like I remember having albums with him and Joe Farrell — two tenors?
Was that a situation that you were in when you played with him? Like no chordal instrument?

No this particular thing — he wasn’t even leading the thing it was like he was a side person like myself but so it was like really a great combination of people: Gary Bartz, Christian McBride, Kenny Werner, so it was kind of a cool thing. It was like three horns, rhythm section, and he was on it, this singer Roseanna Vitro, and it was like, so we started talking and so we’re both from the Detroit area, talking about — he’s older than me obviously but people that he knew and that I played with when I was growing up, and so it was just a great thing. And he was such a sweet person. And he was like, you know, © Fillius Jazz Archive -12-

“We’re going on the road soon, give her your number.” Because we need — because it was like between saxophone players. It was after Pat LaBarbera had stopped playing with him, who was a great musician from Upstate New York. And it was just like I wasn’t ready. In my mind I wasn’t — first of all I’d never be ready. He’s Elvin Jones. But man, I’m glad I got the experience and I would have loved to have played six nights a week.
